description: Questions a downstream reasoner might be asked about the health effects of eggs, authored from corpus/eggs/posts. The cluster's cruxes are about ways of knowing (cohorts vs trials, confounding, subgroups), so the probe reads whether a reasoner keeps the population scope and evidence-quality caveats the record carries (#334 S5). Diagnostic only.

questions.question: Does eating up to one egg a day increase heart disease risk in healthy adults?
questions.note: Mostly null in cohorts for healthy people; the record should keep the 'healthy' scope.

questions.question: Does eating eggs daily increase cardiovascular risk in people with diabetes?
questions.note: The subgroup where the evidence diverges; the record should hold an elevated-risk claim for diabetics.

questions.question: Why did the 2015–2020 US Dietary Guidelines drop the 300 mg/day dietary cholesterol limit?
questions.note: Weak and variable effect of dietary cholesterol on blood cholesterol for most people.

questions.question: Which raises blood cholesterol more: dietary cholesterol or saturated fat?
questions.note: Saturated fat; McGee and the Harvard source agree.

questions.question: Should I trust the randomized trials showing eggs raise LDL, or the observational cohorts showing no association with heart disease in healthy people?
questions.note: The biomarker-vs-hard-outcome crux; the record should carry both and the reason they differ.

questions.question: What is the crux behind the conflicting meta-analyses on eggs and cardiovascular disease?
questions.note: Study selection and reliance on observational data with uncontrolled confounding.

questions.question: Does the TMAO pathway establish that eggs cause heart disease?
questions.note: Proposed mechanism with a confounding/reverse-causation caveat (diabetes and kidney disease raise TMAO).

questions.question: How confident should I be that the observed associations between egg consumption and heart disease are explained by confounding?
questions.note: Contested; the record should hold a middling credence.

questions.question: How confident should I be that adding eggs to a diet raises LDL cholesterol relative to eating no eggs?
questions.note: Consistent trial evidence; the record should hold it as verified/supported with high credence — but only relative to a no-egg diet.

questions.question: How confident should I be that eggs are healthier than red or processed meat as a protein source?
questions.note: The Harvard bottom line; a comparative claim the record may hold as supported.
